note: Establish a broad-cut skeleton and measure actual separation and cost before investing in purity.
notebook:
PLAN: Start a low-cost three-column skeleton (C4-/C5+, then C3-/C4 and C5/C6+); inspect splits, purity and costs, then deepen only high-value branches. Step 1 baseline.
Feed value concentrated in C5-C8; blends can save columns. Initial settings deliberately moderate because costs are high.

note: Sharpen the root, remove ethane from the C3 blend, and test saleable C3/C4/C5 blends with four columns.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a blend-oriented train: root C4-/C5+, light-end ethane/C3 mix/C4 mix, and heavy-end C5/C6+ split; then add C6 and C7-C9 separations only where profitable. Step 2: establish first saleable products.
Baseline root at 50/3/3/.1 leaked substantial C5 overhead and cost $195M; all streams unsold. C3, C4 and C5 blends sacrifice little versus pure values and avoid difficult separations. Sharpen root modestly, split ethane from C3 mix, and test C5 blend purity before expanding heavy branch.

note: Use the proven light-end arrangement, sharpen the C4/C5 root split, and remove the extra C5 column to test a compact saleable blend train.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a five-column blend train: root C4-/C5+, T C3-/C4, TT ethane/C3 mix, and B C5 mix/C6+; establish saleable C3/C4/C5 products, then expand only into profitable heavy cuts. Step 2: sharpen root and validate the core train.
R57 proves the ethane/C3 column can sell C3 mix cheaply. Its root leaks too much C5 overhead and C4 into B, preventing C4/C5 sales. Adopt its effective light-end settings, remove the unproductive BT column, and raise root reflux/boil-up to 4 while retaining 60 stages and 0.1 pressure drop.

note: Test a single-column C5 side draw to capture the largest blend value without paying for a separation tree.
notebook:
PLAN: Test whether a single three-outlet root can make the high-value C5 blend directly; if successful, tune its cut and add only low-cost light/heavy product branches. Step 1: C5 side-draw proof.
The symmetric tree is uneconomic: five columns cost $451M but only C3 sells. R104 shows asymmetric C4/C5 operation sharply lowers root cost, but its two-column descendant still lacks clean cuts. A root side draw could avoid two full columns and target ~695 mol/s C5 worth roughly $600M/yr. Use 80 stages, R=B=5, dp=.2 and a 21% liquid draw just below feed.

note: Replace the failed side-draw concept with the proven two-column C5 blend train and raise root boil-up to keep butane out of the C5 product.
notebook:
PLAN: Build the smallest high-value blend train: sharp root C4/C5 then C5/C6 paraffin. First obtain one saleable C5 blend, then add C6 paraffin/naphthene-heavy only if marginal economics justify it.
R198 showed root 80/8/3 leaves 13% N-butane in BT, the only barrier to C5 sale; its B column already excludes DMB completely. Root 80/5/5 instead pushed Isopentane overhead. Root 80/8/5 should keep C5 down while driving N-butane overhead. R197 B=80/10/3 excludes C6 and yields 630 mol/s C5-rich tops, so reuse it. Expected C5 revenue about $0.62B/yr against roughly $0.5B cost; discard all other streams rather than pay for low-value separations.

note: Strip dimethylbutane from the C5 tops with stronger reboil; this directly targets the only major purity defect.
notebook:
PLAN: First make the C5 blend saleable in the existing two-column train, then reduce root/B cost while preserving 95% purity; add other products only if clearly profitable.
Current root 80/8/5 gives B feed with only 58 mol/s isopentane but all 442 N-pentane; B 80/10/3 gives 556 mol/s tops containing about 473 C5 (85%) and 72 DMB (13%). DMB is the sole important contaminant. Stronger B boil-up should strip DMB into BB while retaining C5 overhead. A saleable C5 tops would earn about $425M/yr, so this is the shortest route to revenue. Root cost ($357M) remains excessive and must later be reduced by fewer stages/lower reflux once a viable purity point is established.

note: Correct the separation direction: lower the second column's boil-up to keep DMB and heavier components out of the C5 blend, while cutting both columns' energy and size.
notebook: PLAN: Establish a low-cost two-column C5 blend train, then add C4 recovery only if the base plant is profitable. Key correction: increasing B boil-up sends MORE DMB/C6 overhead and worsens C5 purity. Earlier B 80/10/3 produced 85% C5 with DMB the main contaminant; lower boil-up should reject heavies. Root 80/8/5 retained all N-pentane but lost much isopentane. Now test root 60/5/2 and B 60/6/1.5, sharply reducing energy and capital. C5 blend revenue ceiling is about $425M/yr, so costs must stay well below that. Do not pursue high-boil-up stripping again.

note: Sharpen the C4/C5 split with more rectification and intermediate boil-up, while keeping the second column's heavy rejection strong.
notebook: PLAN: First obtain one saleable, high-value C5 blend; only then add other recovery branches. Current root loses 165 mol/s N-butane into B, which alone prevents C5 sale. Increase root stages/reflux versus the cheap 60/5/2 run and use boil-up 3.0 as an intermediate between 2.0 (butane leakage) and 5.0 (isopentane loss). Keep B boil-up low at 1.0 so DMB/C6 stays in BB. Target BT at least 95% isopentane+N-pentane. C5 blend gross value is about $618M/yr, enough to pay for two disciplined columns. Side draws and high-boil-up stripping have both failed; do not repeat them.

note: Raise root boil-up to drive the remaining N-butane overhead while retaining the second column's effective heavy-component rejection.
notebook:
PLAN: Obtain the first saleable product via the two-column C5 train. Step 1: eliminate root N-butane leakage by raising root boil-up from 3.0 to 4.5 while retaining the proven 80/8 rectification. Keep B at 60/6/1.0, which already rejects DMB/C6. If C4 remains, polish BT with a small third column; if isopentane loss is excessive, back off slightly. Then measure net value before adding branches.
Current BT at root boil-up 3 is 74% C5, with 24% N-butane and only 2% DMB: root leakage is the controlling defect. R433 confirms heavier B settings merely move the same butane around and add cost. Side draws and high-boil-up stripping failed. C5 blend gross is roughly $260M/yr for the current recovered C5, so avoid unnecessary stages elsewhere.

note: Cut root capital and energy sharply, and trade some C5 recovery for the purity needed to obtain the first saleable product.
notebook:
PLAN: Abandon the costly 80-stage root. Build a low-cost C5-blend train: root removes C4 and lighter, B rejects DMB and heavier. First test 40/4/4 at root and 60/6/0.4 at B; then adjust only the limiting split. A saleable C5 stream can be worth several hundred $M/yr, so total column cost must be kept well below that.
The 80/8/4.5 root costs $333M/yr by itself and cannot yield a profitable plant. Previous B=60/6/1 gave 77% C5, with DMB/C6 leakage; lowering boil-up should improve purity. C5 recovery will fall, but purity and cost take priority now. No revenue has yet been achieved in 22 solves.

note: Switch to the high-value heavy end: isolate octane plus nonane in a small root bottoms stream, then split them into two pure products.
notebook: PLAN: Switch from the unprofitable C5 train to the heavy end. Step 1: make a heptane/octane root cut, then split the small bottoms into octane and nonane. Step 2: tune only purity-limiting settings and reduce cost. The heavy products are worth about $463M/yr combined and should be much easier to purify than close-boiling C5/C6 cuts. A small bottoms flow also makes the finishing column cheap. Use moderate root duty; high reflux is unnecessary because the light tops need not meet specification.

note: Use the observed relationship between root boil-up and cut point: raise boil-up sharply to isolate the C8/C9 bottoms, then split them.
notebook: PLAN: Heavy-end train. Step 1: force a true C8/C9 root split with high boil-up, then split the small bottoms into octane and nonane. Step 2: reduce root duty/cost while retaining saleable purity. R582 showed that boil-up 0.5 strips almost nothing overhead; R584 showed boil-up 4.5 makes a C5/C6 split. Thus the heavy cut needs roughly 12, not the failed low-duty settings. Octane+nonane are worth about $463M/yr, and the finishing column should be small.

note: Reverse the separation route: reject C4 and lighter in the root tops, then distill the C5 blend from the much less volatile bottoms.
notebook: PLAN: Switch to a C4/C5 root split, then recover the valuable C5 blend overhead from the root bottoms. Step 1: establish the cut and C5 purity. Step 2: tune boil-up/recovery and reduce cost. Heavy-end plan failed because high root boil-up still left a large mixed bottoms and root cost exceeded product value. R632/R630 show boil-up 4.5 gives a C5/C6 split, so lower boil-up should move the cut toward C4/C5. C5 blend can earn about $610M/yr; avoid the prior overhead route where butane contaminated the product.

note: Copy the only revenue-positive island design and cut both columns' stages and reflux roughly in half; this directly targets its dominant cost while preserving the proven split settings.
notebook: PLAN: Adopt the proven R676 C5-blend train, then aggressively reduce column cost while preserving the C4/C5 cut and C5 purity. Step 1: test compact columns with the same boil-up ratios. Step 2: tune recovery and finishing-column cost. R676 earns $426.5M/yr but costs $541.4M; its 50/60 stages and reflux 5 are excessive for a blend. Root boil-up 4.5 sets C5/C6 split; finishing boil-up 12 rejects C4 overhead. Compact columns should preserve much of this separation.

note: Remove the zero-revenue C4/C5 column. Keeping only the root and the saleable C6-paraffin branch should turn the current design profitable immediately.
notebook: PLAN: Retain the profitable C6-paraffin branch and remove every auxiliary column whose products are unsold. Step 1: delete the C4/C5 finishing column, which earns no revenue and costs $187.9M/yr. Step 2: reduce root and C6-column duties/stages while protecting the saleable BT blend. Current root+B costs $448.8M/yr against $535.8M revenue, so deleting T should yield about +0.20 reward. The C6 blend is the only demonstrated revenue stream; heavy and light cuts are not worth further separation at these costs.

note: Copy R770's proven two-blend separation and remove all pressure drops. This targets its large refrigeration/utility cost while preserving the successful reflux and boil-up settings.
notebook: PLAN: Start from R770, the island’s proven two-blend plant (reward 0.791), then attack utility costs without changing its successful cut points. Step 1: reproduce its root/T/B settings but operate all columns at feed pressure; R724 showed pressure-drop removal can sharply reduce column cost. Step 2: if purity holds, reduce stages/reflux selectively; if not, revert and optimize only the least purity-sensitive column. R770 earns $577.1M C5 + $634.5M C6 and spends $864.8M. Its unsold TT and BB should remain unsold unless a low-cost finishing opportunity appears.

note: Restore the proven R770 separation while moderately reducing stages and reflux in all columns; retain its essential pressure drops.
notebook: PLAN: Restore R770’s proven pressure levels and cut points, then reduce capital/energy moderately in all three columns. Current step: test 40-stage root and 50-stage finishers with modestly lower reflux. Pressure-drop removal destroyed the separation, so dp must remain 0.5/0.3/0.3. R770 earns $1211.6M/yr from C5 and C6-paraffin blends at $864.8M cost; any purity loss will be addressed by reverting and reducing only one column at a time.

note: Restore the best proven R865 configuration before making any further changes.
notebook: PLAN: Restore R865 immediately, then test only isolated cost reductions while retaining both blends. Current step: secure the proven reward 1.069 baseline. R865 has 50/5/5.5/0.5 root, 60/8/12/0.3 C5 finisher, 45/6/3/0.3 C6 finisher. Broad simultaneous cuts failed badly; purity is highly sensitive. C6 reduced to 45 stages and reflux 6 is safe and saves about $14M; focus next on root/C5 and alternative high-value separations.

note: Test a modest C5-finisher height reduction while holding both operating ratios fixed, avoiding the recovery loss seen when stages and reflux were cut together.
notebook: PLAN: Optimize the proven R865 plant with isolated changes; retain the 1.069 baseline if a trial loses purity. Step 1: reduce only C5-finisher stages from 60 to 50, preserving reflux 8 and boil-up 12. R913 showed that simultaneously cutting stages to 45 and reflux to 6.5 lost $54.5M revenue for only $24.9M savings, so operating ratios may be critical. Current targets are the $382.9M root and $285.6M C5 column; TT and BB are too dilute for economical finishing. If this works, test mild root pressure-drop increases to reduce refrigeration cost.

note: Secure the island's best proven design before further tuning. Its relaxed C6 column recovers substantially more blend without losing the 95% specification.
notebook: PLAN: Secure R957's 1.236 design, then use remaining solves on isolated root-cost reductions while preserving its C6 finisher. R957 improves reward by 0.166 over R915: B at 35/5/3 recovers 66 mol/s more C6 product (+$63.9M) and saves $9.4M. Do not relax B further: BT is already exactly 95% C6 paraffins, so more heavies overhead could erase all $806M. T at 50 gives the same product as 60 but saves only $0.7M; retain proven 60. Next test root 45 stages at unchanged 5/5.5/0.5, then revert if either blend loses specification.

note: Reduce the C5 finisher boil-up while holding its proven reflux and height; TB has purity margin and this column's energy cost is large.
notebook: PLAN: Preserve R957's 1.236 baseline and spend the last six solves on isolated duty reductions in the expensive C5 finisher, then the root if worthwhile. B at 35/5/3 is on the exact 95% C6 boundary; R998 shows 30/4.5 destroys all $806M, so never relax B. Root 45 stages saves almost nothing. T costs $285.6M with boil-up 12 and TB has 98% C5, leaving purity margin. First test boil-up 10.5 at fixed stages/reflux to trade a little C5 recovery for lower energy; revert immediately if reward falls.

note: Restore the proven island-best R1032 exactly after the failed C5 boil-up change. This secures its 1.274 reward and avoids spending a solve on already simulated columns.
notebook: PLAN: Secure R1032's island-best 1.274 now, then use remaining solves only for low-risk isolated cost reductions. R1032 differs from R957 solely in B reflux 4.8 versus 5.0: this saves $2.1M/yr and recovers 15 mol/s more C6 blend while remaining sellable, so it strictly dominates. The T boil-up 10.5 attempt failed convergence and must not be retried. B at 30/4.5 and root at 45/4.5 destroy revenue; preserve all other R1032 settings.

note: Make one very small C6-column reflux reduction at fixed height and cut point. The prior 5.0-to-4.8 change improved both recovery and cost, so 4.7 is the best isolated final probe.
notebook: PLAN: Secure R1032's island-best 1.274, then use remaining solves only for low-risk isolated cost/recovery improvements. Step: probe C6 reflux 4.7 at fixed stages and boil-up. R1032's change from B reflux 5.0 to 4.8 saved $2.1M/yr and recovered 15 mol/s more C6 blend while remaining sellable, gaining 0.038 reward. A further small cut may continue that trend, but R998 showed a purity cliff exists. T reflux 7.5 lost more C5 revenue than it saved; T boil-up 10.5 failed convergence. Preserve root and T settings.

note: Interpolate cautiously between the best C6 reflux settings (4.8 and 4.7); 4.6 is known to cross the blend-purity cliff, so 4.75 offers a low-risk chance of further savings and recovery.
notebook: PLAN: Preserve the proven 1.294 design and use the last three solves on isolated, low-risk refinements. Step: test C6 reflux 4.75, midway between the successful 4.8/4.7 settings. B reflux 4.7 improved recovery by 8 mol/s and cost by $1M/yr versus 4.8, while 4.6 crossed the C6 blend purity cliff and lost $828.7M/yr revenue. Thus 4.75 is the safest remaining interpolation. Preserve root and T: T reflux 7.5 reduced revenue excessively and T boil-up 10.5 failed convergence. If 4.75 remains valid and improves, use remaining solves only for similarly local refinements; otherwise revert to 4.7.

note: Adopt the proven 1.304 configuration exactly before spending the final solve. Its C6 reflux of 4.65 improves recovery and cost while retaining blend purity.
notebook: PLAN: Secure the island-best 1.304 design now, then use the final solve only for a narrowly bracketed C6 reflux probe. Step: copy R1118 exactly (C6 reflux 4.65), replacing the inferior 4.75 interpolation. R1118 raises C6 recovery to 720 mol/s, revenue to $1409.6M/yr, and lowers cost to $837.7M/yr while preserving blend purity. The known cliff lies between 4.65 (valid) and 4.60 (zero C6 revenue); root and T settings remain fixed because earlier T changes lost revenue or failed convergence. If this copy is secured, one final probe at 4.64 may add a small gain, but any failure leaves 1.304 as best.

note: Use the final solve at C6 reflux 4.64, just above the known purity failure at 4.62 and below the proven 4.65 optimum.
notebook: PLAN: Spend the final solve on the last narrowly bracketed C6 reflux probe, then stop with the best valid design secured. R1118 at 4.65 gives reward 1.304, $1409.6M/yr revenue and $837.7M/yr cost. R1146 at 4.62 loses C6 blend purity and all BT revenue, so the cliff is tightly bracketed. Probe 4.64: it may slightly improve recovery and cost, while the already evaluated 4.65 design remains the fallback best. Root and T are fixed; earlier changes there lost revenue or failed convergence.
